section.heading: 10.4. Calculus in Polar Coordinates
section.paragraph: In this section we apply the methods of calculus to find areas, arc lengths, and tangents involving polar curves.
section.heading: Area
section.paragraph: To develop the formula for the area of a region whose boundary is given by a polar equation, we need to use the formula for the area of a sector of a circle:

where, as in Figure 1, $$r$$ is the radius and $$\theta$$ is the radian measure of the central angle. Formula 1 follows from the fact that the area of a sector is proportional to its central angle: $$A = (\theta \slash 2\pi)\pi r^{2} = \frac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta$$ . (See also Exercise 7.3.41.)

image.alt: The figure is a sector of radius r and angle theta. The area within the sector is shaded.

section.paragraph: Let $$\mathcal{R}$$ be the region, illustrated in Figure 2, bounded by the polar curve $$r = f(\theta)$$ and by the rays $$\theta = a$$ and $$\theta = b$$ , where $$f$$ is a positive continuous function and where $$0 < b - a \leqslant 2\pi$$ . We divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into subintervals with endpoints $$\theta_{0},\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\ldots,\theta_{n}$$ and equal width $$\Delta\theta$$ . The rays $$\theta = \theta_{i}$$ then divide $$\mathcal{R}$$ into $$n$$ smaller regions with central angle $$\Delta\theta = \theta_{i} - \theta_{i - 1}$$ . If we choose $$\theta_{i}^{\ast}$$ in the $$i$$ th subinterval $$\left\lbrack {\theta_{i - 1},\theta_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ , then the area $$\Delta A_{i}$$ of the $$i$$ th region is approximated by the area of the sector of a circle with central angle $$\Delta\theta$$ and radius $$f\left( \theta_{i}^{\ast} \right)$$ . (See Figure 3.)

The region bound by the curve and the second and third rays is shaded and labeled R.

section.paragraph: Thus from Formula 1 we have
$$\Delta A_{i} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f\left( \theta_{i}^{\ast} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta\theta$$
and so an approximation to the total area $$A$$ of $$\mathcal{R}$$ is
$$A \approx \underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack f\left( \theta_{i}^{*} \right) \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta\theta}$$

It appears from Figure 3 that the approximation in (2) improves as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . But the sums in (2) are Riemann sums for the function $$g(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}$$ , so

$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f\left( \theta_{i}^{\ast} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta\theta = {\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}d\theta}}}$$
It therefore appears plausible (and can in fact be proved) that the formula for the area $$A$$ of the polar region $$\mathcal{R}$$ is
$$A = {\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}d\theta}}$$
Formula 3 is often written as
with the understanding that $$r = f(\theta)$$ . Note the similarity between Formulas 1 and 4.
When we apply Formula 3 or 4, it is helpful to think of the area as being swept out by a rotating ray through $$O$$ that starts with angle $$a$$ and ends with angle $$b$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the area enclosed by one loop of the four-leaved rose $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ .

Solution The curve $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ was sketched in Example 10.3.8. Notice from Figure 4 that the region enclosed by the right loop is swept out by a ray that rotates from $$\theta = - \pi \slash 4$$ to $$\theta = \pi \slash 4$$ . Therefore Formula 3 gives
$$A = {\int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}{\frac{1}{2}r^{2}d\theta = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}{\cos^{2}2\theta d\theta}}}}$$

image.alt: Details A function, two lines, a shaded region, and an arrow are graphed on a coordinate plane. The function is a four-leaved rose labeled r = cos(2 theta). The leaves of the rose are along the positive and negative axes, symmetric about them. A dashed line slopes upward to the right from the origin and exits at the top right and is labeled theta = pi/4. Another dashed line slopes down to the right from the origin and exits at the bottom right and is labeled theta = negative pi/4. The leaf along the positive horizontal axis is shaded. An arrow begins from the origin and slopes downward to the right until it meets the lower half of the shaded leaf.

example.paragraph: Because the region is symmetric about the polar axis $$\theta = 0$$ , we can write

$$\begin{array}{ll} {A = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\cos^{2}2\theta d\theta} & \\ {\phantom{A} = \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 4\theta)d\theta} & { \left\lbrack \text{because} \cos^{2}u = \frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2u) \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{A} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack \theta + \frac{1}{4}\sin 4\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi/4} = \frac{\pi}{8}} & \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the area of the region that lies inside the circle $$r = 3\sin\theta$$ and outside the cardioid $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ .

Solution The cardioid (see Example 10.3.7) and the circle are sketched in Figure 5 and the desired region is shaded. The values of $$a$$ and $$b$$ in Formula 3 are determined by finding the points of intersection of the two curves. They intersect when $$3\sin\theta = 1 + \sin\theta$$ . This gives $$\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}$$ , so $$\theta = \pi \slash 6$$ , $$5\pi \slash 6$$ . The desired area can be found by subtracting the area inside the cardioid between $$\theta = \pi \slash 6$$ and $$\theta = 5\pi \slash 6$$ from the area inside the circle from $$\pi \slash 6$$ to $$5\pi \slash 6$$ . Thus
$$A = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{5\pi \slash 6}{\left( {3\sin\theta} \right)^{2}d\theta - \frac{1}{2}{\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{5\pi \slash 6}{\left( {1 + \sin\theta} \right)^{2}d\theta}}}}$$
Since the region is symmetric about the vertical axis $$\theta = \pi \slash 2$$ , we can write

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {2\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{9\sin^{2}\theta d\theta - \frac{1}{2}{\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{{({1 + 2\sin\theta + \sin^{2}\theta})}d\theta}}}}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{{({8{\sin}^{2}\theta - 1 - 2\sin\theta})}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{\left( {3 - 4\cos 2\theta - 2\sin\theta} \right)d\theta}} \left\lbrack {because}\sin^{2}\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - \cos 2\theta} \right) \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{A} = {3\theta - 2\sin 2\theta + 2\cos\theta}{\rbrack_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{= \pi}}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Example 2 illustrates the procedure for finding the area of the region bounded by two polar curves. In general, let $$\mathcal{R}$$ be a region, as illustrated in Figure 6, that is bounded by curves with polar equations $$r = f(\theta)$$ , $$r = g(\theta)$$ , $$\theta = a$$ , and $$\theta = b$$ , where $$f(\theta) \geqslant g(\theta) \geqslant 0$$ and $$0 < b - a \leqslant 2\pi$$ . The area $$A$$ of $$\mathcal{R}$$ is found by subtracting the area inside $$r = g(\theta)$$ from the area inside $$r = f(\theta)$$ , so using Formula 3 we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}d\theta - {\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {g(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}d\theta}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{a}^{b}{{({\left\lbrack {f(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2} - \left\lbrack {g(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}})}d\theta}}}} \end{array}$$

The first line segment, labeled theta = a slopes gradually upward to the right from O at an angle a from the horizontal ray. The second line segment, labeled theta = b, slopes steeply upward to the right at an angle b from the horizontal ray. The region bound by the two curves and the line segment theta = b is shaded and labeled R.

section.paragraph: Caution The fact that a single point has many representations in polar coordinates sometimes makes it difficult to find all the points of intersection of two polar curves. For instance, it is obvious from Figure 5 that the circle and the cardioid have three points of intersection; however, in Example 2 we solved the equations $$r = 3\sin\theta$$ and $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ and found only two such points, $$\left( {\frac{3}{2},\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ and $$\left( {\frac{3}{2},5\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ . The origin is also a point of intersection, but we can’t find it by solving the equations of the curves because the origin has no single representation in polar coordinates that satisfies both equations. Notice that, when represented as $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ or $$\left( {0,\pi} \right)$$ , the origin satisfies $$r = 3\sin\theta$$ and so it lies on the circle; when represented as $$\left( {0,3\pi \slash 2} \right)$$ , it satisfies $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ and so it lies on the cardioid. Think of two points moving along the curves as the parameter value $$\theta$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$2\pi$$ . On one curve the origin is reached at $$\theta = 0$$ and $$\theta = \pi$$ ; on the other curve it is reached at $$\theta = 3\pi \slash 2$$ . The points don’t collide at the origin because they reach the origin at different times, but the curves intersect there nonetheless. (See also Exercises 10.1.55, 10.1.56, and 10.1.57.)

Thus, to find all points of intersection of two polar curves, it is recommended that you draw the graphs of both curves. It is especially convenient to use a graphing calculator or computer to help with this task.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find all points of intersection of the curves $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ and $$r = \frac{1}{2}$$ .

Solution If we solve the equations $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ and $$r = \frac{1}{2}$$ simultaneously, we get $$\cos 2\theta = \frac{1}{2}$$ and, therefore, $$2\theta = \pi \slash 3$$ , $$5\pi \slash 3$$ , $$7\pi \slash 3$$ , $$11\pi \slash 3$$ . Thus the values of $$\theta$$ between $$0$$ and $$2\pi$$ that satisfy both equations are $$\theta = \pi \slash 6$$ , $$5\pi \slash 6$$ , $$7\pi \slash 6$$ , $$11\pi \slash 6$$ . We have found four points of intersection: $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},5\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},7\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},11\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ .

However, you can see from Figure 7 that the curves have four other points of intersection—namely, $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},2\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},4\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},5\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ . These can be found using symmetry or by noticing that another equation of the circle is $$r = - \frac{1}{2}$$ and then solving the equations $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ and $$r = - \frac{1}{2}$$ simultaneously.

The circle labeled r = 1/2, has its center at the origin and crosses the upper half of the left leaf at a point labeled (1/2, pi/6) and the right half of the top leaf at a point labeled (1/2, pi/3).

section.heading: Arc Length
section.paragraph: Recall from Section 10.3 that rectangular coordinates $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ are related by the equations $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , $$x = r\sin\theta$$ . Regarding $$\theta$$ as a parameter allows us to write parametric equations for a polar curve $$r = f(\theta)$$ as follows.
$$x = r\cos\theta = f(\theta)\cos\theta y = r\sin\theta = f(\theta)\sin\theta$$
Parametric equations for a polar curve
To find the length of a polar curve $$r = f(\theta)$$ , $$a \leqslant \theta \leqslant b$$ , we start with Equations 5 and differentiate with respect to $$\theta$$ (using the Product Rule):
$$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta - r\sin\theta \frac{dy}{d\theta} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta + r\cos\theta$$
Then, using $$\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta = 1$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left( \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{d\theta} \right)^{2} = \left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2}\cos^{2}\theta - 2r\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta\sin\theta + r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta} \\ {{+ \left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2}\sin^{2}\theta + 2r\frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta\cos\theta + r^{2}{\cos}^{2}\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\left( \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{d\theta} \right)^{2}} = {\left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + r^{2}}} \end{array}$$
Assuming that $$f^{\prime}$$ is continuous, we can use Theorem 10.2.5 to write the arc length as
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{d\theta} \right)^{2}}d\theta}}$$
Therefore the length of a curve with polar equation $${r = f(\theta)},{a \leqslant \theta \leqslant b}$$ , is
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{r^{2} + \left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2}}d\theta}}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the length of the cardioid $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ .
Solution The cardioid is shown in Figure 8. (We sketched it in Example 10.3.7.) Its full length is given by the parameter interval $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , so Formula 6 gives

$$L = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{r^{2} + \left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2}}d\theta = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{\left( {1 + \sin\theta} \right)^{2} + \cos^{2}\theta^{}}d\theta = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{2 + 2\sin\theta^{}}d\theta}}}}}}$$

We could evaluate this integral by multiplying and dividing the integrand by $$\sqrt{2 - 2\sin\theta}$$ , or we could use mathematical software. In any event, we find that the length of the cardioid is $$L = 8$$ .

image.alt: Details A cardioid with its cusp opening downward is graphed on a coordinate plane. The pointed end of the cusp is at the origin, labeled O.

section.heading: Tangents
section.paragraph: To find a tangent line to a polar curve $$r = f(\theta)$$ , we again regard $$\theta$$ as a parameter and write parametric equations for the curve following Equations 5:
$$x = r\cos\theta = f(\theta)\cos\theta y = r\sin\theta = f(\theta)\sin\theta$$
Then, using the method for finding the slope of a parametric curve (Equation 10.2.1) and the Product Rule, we have
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{d\theta}}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}} = \frac{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}$$

We locate horizontal tangents by finding the points where $$dy \slash d\theta = 0$$ (provided that $$dx \slash d\theta \neq 0$$ ). Likewise, we locate vertical tangents at the points where $$dx \slash d\theta = 0$$ (provided that $$dy \slash d\theta \neq 0$$ ).
Notice that if we are looking for tangent lines at the pole, then $$r = 0$$ and Equation 7 simplifies to
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \tan\theta {if}\frac{dr}{d\theta} \neq 0$$

For instance, in Example 10.3.8 we found that $$r = \cos 2\theta = 0$$ when $$\theta = \pi \slash 4$$ or $$3\pi \slash 4$$ . This means that the lines $$\theta = \pi \slash 4$$ and $$\theta = 3\pi \slash 4$$ (or $$y = x$$ and $$y = - x$$ ) are tangent lines to $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ at the origin.

example.heading: Example 5

list.item: (a) For the cardioid $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ of Example 4, find the slope of the tangent line when $$\theta = \pi \slash 3$$ .
(b) Find the points on the cardioid where the tangent line is horizontal or vertical.

example.paragraph: Solution Using Equation 7 with $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta - r\sin\theta} = \frac{\cos\theta\sin\theta + \left( 1 + \sin\theta \right)\cos\theta}{\cos\theta\cos\theta - \left( 1 + \sin\theta \right)\sin\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dy}{dx}} = \frac{\cos\theta\left( {1 + 2\sin\theta} \right)}{1 - 2{\sin}^{2}\theta - \sin\theta} = \frac{\cos\theta\left( {1 + 2\sin\theta} \right)}{\left( {1 + \sin\theta} \right)\left( {1 - 2\sin\theta} \right)}} \end{array}$$

list.item: (a) The slope of the tangent at the point where $$\theta = \pi \slash 3$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {\left. \frac{dy}{dx} \right|_{\theta = \pi \slash 3} = \frac{\cos\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right)\left\lbrack {1 + 2\sin\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right)} \right\rbrack}{\left\lbrack {1 + \sin\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right)} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack {1 - 2\sin\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right)} \right\rbrack} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \sqrt{3}} \right)}{\left( {1 + \sqrt{3} \slash 2} \right)\left( {1 - \sqrt{3}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\left. \frac{dy}{dx} \right|_{\theta = \pi \slash 3}} = \frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{\left( {2 + \sqrt{3}} \right)\left( {1 - \sqrt{3}} \right)} = {\frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{- 1 - \sqrt{3}} = - 1}} \end{array}$$

example.paragraph: Therefore there are horizontal tangents at the points $$\left( {2,\pi \slash 2} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},7\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},11\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ and vertical tangents at $$\left( {\frac{3}{2},\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ and $$\left( {\frac{3}{2},5\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ . When $$\theta = 3\pi \slash 2$$ , both $$dy \slash d\theta$$ and $$dx \slash d\theta$$ are $$0$$ , so we must be careful. Using l’Hospital’s Rule, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{dy}{dx} = \left( {\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{1 + 2\sin\theta}{1 - 2\sin\theta}} \right)\left( {\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{\cos\theta}{1 + \sin\theta}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{dy}{dx}}{= - \frac{1}{3}\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{\cos\theta}{1 + \sin\theta} = - \frac{1}{3}\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{- \sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \infty}} \end{array}$$
By symmetry,
$$\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{+}}\frac{dy}{dx} = - \infty$$
Thus there is a vertical tangent line at the pole (see Figure 9).

section.paragraph: Note Instead of having to remember Equation 7, we could employ the method used to derive it. For instance, in Example 5 we could have written parametric equations for the curve as
$$\begin{array}{l} {x = r\cos\theta = (1 + \sin\theta)\cos\theta = \cos\theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta} \\ {y = r\sin\theta = (1 + \sin\theta)\sin\theta = \sin\theta + \sin^{2}\theta} \end{array}$$
Then we have

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy \slash d\theta}{dx \slash d\theta} = \frac{\cos\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{- \sin\theta + \cos 2\theta} = \frac{\cos\theta + \sin 2\theta}{- \sin\theta + \cos 2\theta}$$
which is equivalent to our previous expression.
